title: The Bench Beside the River
passage:
Every afternoon, Nao walked home along a narrow river. Most days he hurried because he wanted to reach home before his favorite radio program began. One Tuesday, however, he noticed an old wooden bench under a tree. He had passed it many times, but he had never stopped there. The sun was warm, and he was tired after carrying sports equipment at school, so he sat down for a few minutes.

From the bench, the river looked different. Nao could see small fish moving near the stones. A white bird stood in the shallow water and waited without moving. On the other side of the river, a man was planting flowers beside his house. Nao realized that he had walked this road for almost two years without really seeing these things. He had known the river was there, but he had treated it like part of the background.

The next day, Nao stopped again. This time an older woman was sitting on the bench. She moved her bag and made space for him. They did not talk at first. After a while, she pointed at the water and said that ducks often came in winter. She had lived in the neighborhood for more than thirty years and knew many small changes in the river. She told Nao that there used to be fewer trees, and summer afternoons had felt much hotter.

Nao began stopping at the bench once or twice a week. Sometimes he met the woman, and sometimes he sat alone. He still liked his radio program, but missing the first few minutes no longer seemed important. He started taking pictures of the river with his phone and comparing them from week to week. He noticed when flowers opened, when the water rose after rain, and when leaves began to change color.

By autumn, the bench had become one of his favorite places. It had not changed, but Nao had. He learned that a familiar place can still offer something new when a person slows down enough to notice it. The river had always been beside him. What changed was the attention he gave it.
translation:
毎日午後、ナオは細い川沿いの道を歩いて家に帰っていました。たいていはお気に入りのラジオ番組が始まる前に帰宅したくて急いでいました。ところがある火曜日、木の下に古い木製のベンチがあることに気づきました。何度も通り過ぎていましたが、そこに座ったことはありませんでした。その日は暖かく、学校で運動用具を運んで疲れていたため、数分休むことにしました。

ベンチから見ると、川はいつもと違って見えました。石の近くを泳ぐ小さな魚、浅瀬でじっと待つ白い鳥、川の向こうで家のそばに花を植える男性が見えました。ナオは、ほぼ二年間この道を歩いてきたのに、こうしたものをほとんど見ていなかったことに気づきました。川があることは知っていても、ただ背景の一部として扱っていたのです。

翌日も立ち寄ると、年配の女性が座っていました。女性は荷物を動かして席を空けてくれました。しばらくして、冬になるとカモがよく来ることや、昔は木が少なく夏はもっと暑く感じたことを教えてくれました。彼女はその地域に三十年以上住み、川の小さな変化をよく知っていました。

それからナオは週に一、二度ベンチに立ち寄るようになりました。女性に会う日もあれば、一人で座る日もありました。ラジオ番組は好きなままでしたが、最初の数分を聞き逃すことは気にならなくなりました。スマートフォンで川の写真を撮り、週ごとの変化を比べるようになり、花が咲く時期、雨の後に水位が上がる様子、葉の色が変わる時期にも気づきました。

秋になる頃には、そのベンチはお気に入りの場所の一つになっていました。ベンチ自体が変わったのではありません。変わったのはナオでした。見慣れた場所でも、立ち止まって注意を向ければ新しいものを見つけられることを知ったのです。川はずっとそこにありました。変わったのは、彼がそこへ向ける注意でした。

title: A Map for New Students
passage:
At the beginning of the school year, Mei noticed that first-year students often looked confused in the hallways. The school building was not very large, but several rooms had similar doors, and the signs were small. New students sometimes walked past the science room or turned the wrong way when they were trying to find the library. Mei remembered having the same problem when she first entered the school.

During lunch, she told two friends that the school needed a better map. One friend suggested drawing a simple floor plan, while the other said that a map alone might not be enough. They decided to ask first-year students what was difficult. After speaking with fifteen students, they learned that the biggest problem was not finding classrooms. Most students could find those after a few days. The hardest places were the nurse's office, the music practice rooms, and the stairs that led to the gym balcony.

Mei and her friends made a new map on a large sheet of paper. Instead of using only room numbers, they added small pictures. A red cross showed the nurse's office, a musical note showed the practice rooms, and a basketball showed the way to the gym. They also used arrows to show the shortest routes from the main entrance. Before putting the map on the wall, they asked three new students to test it. Two of the students understood it immediately, but one thought an arrow pointed to the wrong staircase. The group changed the design.

The finished map was placed near the entrance. For the next week, Mei watched people use it. Some students stopped for only a few seconds. Others pointed at the pictures and talked with friends. A teacher later asked if the group could make a smaller version for the school website. Mei was surprised that a simple project had become useful in more than one way.

The experience taught her an important lesson. Good design does not begin with making something attractive. It begins with noticing where people have trouble, asking them about it, and changing an idea after seeing how it works in real life. The map was useful because it was created with its users, not only for them.
translation:
新学期の初め、メイは一年生が廊下で迷っていることが多いと気づきました。校舎はそれほど大きくありませんが、似たような扉が多く、案内表示も小さかったためです。理科室を通り過ぎたり、図書館へ行く途中で反対方向へ曲がったりする生徒もいました。メイ自身も入学したばかりの頃、同じように困ったことを覚えていました。

昼休みに二人の友人へ話すと、一人は簡単な見取り図を描こうと提案し、もう一人は地図だけでは十分でないかもしれないと言いました。そこでまず一年生に何が難しいのか尋ねました。十五人に聞いたところ、意外にも教室を見つけることが最大の問題ではありませんでした。数日たてば教室は覚えられます。最も見つけにくかったのは保健室、音楽の練習室、体育館のバルコニーへ続く階段でした。

三人は大きな紙に新しい地図を作りました。部屋番号だけでなく、保健室には赤い十字、音楽室には音符、体育館にはバスケットボールの絵を加え、正面玄関からの最短経路も矢印で示しました。掲示する前に新入生三人へ試してもらうと、二人はすぐ理解できましたが、一人は矢印が違う階段を示しているように感じました。そこでデザインを直しました。

完成した地図は入口近くに置かれました。メイが一週間様子を見ると、数秒だけ立ち止まる生徒もいれば、絵を指さしながら友人と話す生徒もいました。後には先生から、学校のウェブサイト用に小さい版も作ってほしいと頼まれました。単純な計画がいくつもの形で役立ったことに、メイは驚きました。

この経験から、よいデザインは見た目をきれいにすることから始まるのではないと学びました。人がどこで困るのかに気づき、実際に尋ね、使われ方を見ながら直すことから始まります。その地図が役立ったのは、利用者のためだけでなく、利用者と一緒に作られたからでした。

title: The Cup That Was Used Again
passage:
The student café at Yui's school sold warm drinks during winter. Every morning, many paper cups were placed beside the machine, and by the end of lunch a large trash bag was full of them. Yui did not think much about the cups until the environmental club counted the waste for one week. They found that the school was throwing away more than three hundred cups every five days.

The club suggested that students bring reusable cups. At first, the idea sounded easy. The café could give a small discount to anyone who brought one. However, the staff pointed out two problems. Students sometimes forgot to wash their cups, and different cup sizes made it hard to know how much drink to pour. The club realized that simply telling people to reuse things was not enough. The system had to be convenient.

They tested a new plan for two weeks. The school bought fifty strong plastic cups that could be washed and used again. Students paid a small deposit when they borrowed a cup. If they returned it to a collection box, they received the deposit back. The cups were all the same size, so the café staff could serve drinks quickly. At the end of each day, the cups were washed in the cooking classroom.

The first week was not perfect. Some students forgot to return the cups, and one collection box was placed too far from the main hallway. The club moved the box and added a large sign. After that, the return rate improved. By the third week, the café used less than half as many paper cups as before. Some students also began bringing their own bottles because the project had made them think about waste.

Yui learned that changing a habit often requires more than a good message. People may agree with an idea and still choose the easier option. The reusable cup project worked better when returning a cup was simple and the reward was clear. The biggest change did not come from asking students to care more. It came from making the better choice easier to make every day.
translation:
ユイの学校の生徒カフェでは、冬になると温かい飲み物を販売していました。毎朝たくさんの紙コップが機械の横に並び、昼休みが終わる頃には大きなごみ袋がいっぱいになっていました。環境クラブが一週間のごみを数えるまで、ユイはそれほど気にしていませんでした。調べると、学校では五日間で三百個以上の紙コップを捨てていました。

クラブは再利用できるカップを持参することを提案しました。しかし、カフェの職員から、洗っていないカップを持ってくる生徒がいることや、サイズがばらばらだと飲み物の量を決めにくいことを指摘されました。単に『再利用しよう』と呼びかけるだけでは不十分で、便利な仕組みが必要だと分かりました。

そこで二週間、新しい方法を試しました。学校が同じ大きさの丈夫なプラスチック製カップを五十個用意し、借りるときに少額の保証金を払い、回収箱へ返すと返金される仕組みにしました。大きさが統一されていたため、カフェ側も素早く飲み物を注げました。毎日、調理室で洗って再利用しました。

最初の週はうまくいかない点もありました。返却を忘れる生徒がいたり、回収箱の一つが廊下から遠すぎたりしました。クラブが箱の位置を変え、大きな表示を付けると返却率が上がりました。三週目には紙コップの使用量が以前の半分以下になり、計画をきっかけに自分のボトルを持ってくる生徒も増えました。

ユイは、習慣を変えるには良い呼びかけだけでは足りないことを学びました。考えに賛成していても、人はより楽な選択をしがちです。返却を簡単にし、利点を分かりやすくしたことで計画は成功しました。大きな変化を生んだのは『もっと気にしよう』と求めることではなく、良い選択を毎日しやすくすることでした。

title: Saturday at the Repair Table
passage:
Once a month, the community center near Sota's home held a repair morning. People brought lamps, small chairs, toys, and other household items that no longer worked well. Volunteers sat around several tables with simple tools. They did not promise that everything could be fixed, but they tried to repair safe items instead of throwing them away immediately.

Sota first went there with his grandfather, who had an old desk lamp. The switch worked only when it was pressed at a certain angle. Sota expected the volunteers to replace the whole switch. Instead, a woman named Ms. Mori opened the base and found that one small screw was loose. She tightened it, cleaned the inside, and tested the lamp several times. It worked again. The repair took less than ten minutes.

Sota was surprised because he had assumed that broken objects usually needed new parts. Ms. Mori explained that many problems were simple, but people often could not see the cause from the outside. She also said that some repairs should not be attempted without training, especially when electricity, gas, or dangerous tools were involved. Learning when not to repair something was part of being careful.

The next month, Sota returned as a helper. He was not allowed to repair electrical items, but he could organize screws, label boxes, and help younger children fix simple wooden toys. One boy brought a toy car with a loose wheel. Sota showed him how to look closely at the axle before deciding what to do. Together they found a small piece that had moved out of place. They pushed it back carefully, and the wheel turned again.

By the end of the morning, Sota had not repaired many things himself, yet he felt he had learned a lot. The repair table was not only about saving money or reducing waste. It also changed the way people looked at objects. Instead of asking, ‘Is this broken?’ they began by asking, ‘What exactly is wrong?’ That small change in the question often opened the door to a solution.
translation:
ソウタの家の近くの公民館では、月に一度『修理の朝』が開かれていました。人々は調子の悪くなったランプ、椅子、おもちゃなどを持ち寄り、ボランティアが簡単な工具で、安全に直せるものを捨てる前に修理しようとしていました。もちろん、すべてが直るとは約束していませんでした。

ソウタが初めて行ったのは祖父と一緒で、古い机用ランプを持っていきました。スイッチは特定の角度で押した時しか動きません。ソウタは部品を丸ごと交換すると思いましたが、森さんという女性が土台を開くと、小さなねじが緩んでいるだけでした。締め直し、中を掃除して何度か試すと、十分ほどでまた使えるようになりました。

ソウタは、壊れた物は新しい部品が必要だと思い込んでいたため驚きました。森さんは、原因が外から見えないだけで単純な故障も多いと説明しました。一方で、電気やガス、危険な工具に関わる修理は知識がないまま行うべきではなく、『直さない方がよい場合を知ること』も大切だと話しました。

翌月、ソウタは手伝いとして戻りました。電気製品は扱えませんが、ねじを整理したり箱にラベルを付けたり、子どもの簡単な木製おもちゃを直す手伝いをしました。車のおもちゃの車輪が緩んでいた男の子と一緒に軸をよく調べると、小さな部品がずれていることが分かり、元に戻すと車輪がまた回りました。

その朝、ソウタ自身が直した物は多くありませんでしたが、多くを学びました。修理の場は、お金を節約したりごみを減らしたりするだけの場所ではありません。物の見方も変えてくれます。『これは壊れているか』ではなく、『具体的にどこが悪いのか』と考える。その小さな問いの違いが、解決への入口になることがあるのです。

title: A Window Full of Herbs
passage:
The cooking classroom at Rina's school had a wide window that received sunlight for most of the morning. For years, nothing had been placed there except a few empty containers. When the cooking club began planning spring activities, one student suggested growing herbs in the window. They used small pots and planted basil, mint, parsley, and green onions.

At first, the project seemed simple. The students watered the plants every day and expected all of them to grow quickly. After two weeks, however, the basil was healthy while the parsley was weak. The mint grew so fast that it began covering the soil around another plant. The club realized that different plants did not need exactly the same care. They looked up basic information and moved some pots to places with less direct sun. They also began checking the soil before adding water.

The herbs soon became part of cooking practice. Instead of buying a whole package of parsley for one lesson, the students cut only what they needed. They added basil to tomato soup and mint to cold water with lemon. The amount of food saved was not large, but the students enjoyed seeing where one ingredient came from. It made a recipe feel connected to something living rather than only to packages from a store.

There were failures too. One weekend, the room became unusually hot and several green onion leaves dried out. Another time, tiny insects appeared under the mint leaves. The club solved the problems without using strong chemicals, but the plants never looked perfect. Rina came to understand that this was normal. A real growing space changed from week to week.

By summer, the window had become one of the most noticeable parts of the classroom. Students from other clubs sometimes stopped to smell the mint or ask about the pots. Rina liked the project because it was useful, but she liked something else even more. The plants made the class pay attention. Water, sunlight, temperature, and time could no longer be treated as ideas in a book. They were conditions that had to be observed every day.
translation:
リナの学校の調理室には、午前中の大部分に日が当たる広い窓がありました。長い間、そこには空の容器が少し置かれているだけでした。春の活動を考えていた調理クラブで、窓辺にハーブを育てようという案が出て、バジル、ミント、パセリ、青ねぎを小さな鉢に植えました。

最初は簡単そうでした。毎日水をやれば同じように育つと思っていましたが、二週間後、バジルは元気なのにパセリは弱く、ミントは勢いよく広がりました。植物によって必要な世話が違うと気づき、基本的な育て方を調べ、直射日光の少ない場所へ移したり、水をやる前に土を確認したりするようになりました。

やがてハーブは調理実習でも使われました。一回の授業のためにパセリを一袋買うのではなく、必要な分だけ切り、バジルはトマトスープへ、ミントはレモン入りの冷水へ加えました。節約できる量は大きくありませんでしたが、材料がどこから来たのかを目で見られることを生徒たちは楽しみました。料理が店の包装だけでなく、生きているものにつながっているように感じられたのです。

失敗もありました。週末に室温が高くなり青ねぎの葉が乾いたり、ミントの葉の裏に小さな虫が出たりしました。強い薬品を使わず対処しましたが、植物がいつも完璧に見えることはありませんでした。リナは、それが自然なのだと理解しました。実際の栽培場所は週ごとに変化するものです。

夏には窓辺が教室でも特に目立つ場所になりました。他のクラブの生徒もミントの香りをかいだり、鉢について質問したりしました。リナが一番気に入ったのは、植物がみんなに『注意して見る』ことを教えてくれた点でした。水、日光、気温、時間は、もう本の中の言葉ではなく、毎日観察しなければならない条件になったのです。

title: The Quiet Corner of the Gym
passage:
During the school festival, the gym was one of the busiest places on campus. Music played from speakers, students called to visitors, and several clubs shared the same large room. The energy was exciting, but some visitors found it tiring. A teacher noticed that a few younger children and older guests left the gym after only a short time because there was nowhere quiet to rest.

Before the next festival, Kenta's class was asked to think of a simple improvement. They did not have money for a new room, so they looked at the gym itself. Behind the stage curtain, there was a small side area that was normally used for storing folding chairs. The chairs could be moved to another place for one day. The class decided to turn the area into a quiet corner.

They placed four chairs, two small tables, and a sign that said, ‘Rest Area — Please Keep Voices Low.’ They did not decorate it with flashing lights or loud colors. Instead, they used a few paper plants and soft-colored posters. One student suggested playing quiet music, but another pointed out that true quiet might be more helpful. They chose not to add any sound.

On the festival day, the corner was used more often than expected. A grandmother sat there while waiting for her family. A child who had become tired stayed for ten minutes and then returned to the games. Two students who were helping at booths used the space during their breaks. Nobody stayed for very long, but that was not the purpose. It was a place to pause.

After the festival, the class collected short comments from visitors. Several people said the quiet corner made the gym easier to enjoy because they knew they could step away for a moment. Kenta learned that improving an event does not always mean adding more activities. Sometimes a better experience comes from removing noise, giving people space, or allowing them to choose when to rest. The small corner worked because it offered something the festival had been missing: a little less.
translation:
学校祭の日、体育館は校内でも特に混雑する場所でした。スピーカーから音楽が流れ、生徒が来場者を呼び込み、複数のクラブが同じ広い空間を使っていました。活気は楽しい一方、幼い子どもや年配の来場者の中には、静かに休める場所がなく、短時間で体育館を出る人もいました。

翌年の祭りに向け、ケンタのクラスは簡単な改善案を考えることになりました。新しい部屋を作る予算はありません。そこで体育館を見直すと、舞台のカーテンの裏に、普段は折りたたみ椅子を置く小さな場所がありました。一日だけ椅子を移し、そこを『静かな休憩コーナー』にすることにしました。

椅子四脚、小さなテーブル二つ、『休憩場所―声は小さめに』という表示を置きました。派手な光や強い色は使わず、紙の植物と落ち着いた色のポスターだけにしました。静かな音楽を流す案も出ましたが、本当の静けさの方が役立つかもしれないと考え、音は加えませんでした。

当日は予想以上に利用されました。家族を待つ祖母、疲れて十分ほど休んでから遊びに戻る子ども、出店を手伝う生徒などが使いました。長時間いる人はいませんでしたが、それでよかったのです。そこは立ち止まるための場所でした。

後日、来場者から短い感想を集めると、『少し離れて休める場所があると分かっているだけで、体育館を楽しみやすかった』という声がいくつもありました。ケンタは、催しを良くすることは必ずしも何かを増やすことではないと学びました。音を減らし、空間を作り、休む選択肢を用意することで体験が良くなることもあります。この小さな場所が役立ったのは、祭りに足りなかった『少し少ないこと』を与えたからでした。

title: One More Stop on the Bus
passage:
Haruto took the same bus to school every morning. He usually got off at the stop closest to the school gate. One day, road construction blocked the bus lane, and the driver announced that the usual stop would be closed for a week. Students had to get off one stop earlier and walk about eight extra minutes. Haruto was annoyed because he liked keeping his morning routine exactly the same.

On the first day, he walked quickly and paid little attention to the street. On the second day, rain slowed him down. He noticed a small shop that repaired watches and clocks. Dozens of old clocks could be seen through the window. Some were tall, some were round, and one had a wooden bird that appeared every hour. Haruto had never known the shop existed, even though it was not far from his school.

The next morning, he left home five minutes earlier and stopped outside the shop. An elderly man was opening the door. He saw Haruto looking at the clocks and invited him to look for a minute before school. Haruto learned that the shop had been there for forty years. The man said fewer people repaired clocks now because inexpensive digital devices were easy to replace, but some customers still brought old clocks that had belonged to their families for decades.

During the week, Haruto visited twice more. He did not become an expert, but he learned how a mechanical clock used small gears to move the hands. He also heard stories about clocks that had been gifts, wedding presents, or memories of grandparents. When the road construction ended, the bus returned to its normal route. Haruto could once again get off beside the school gate.

He was glad the shorter walk was back, but he did not completely return to his old routine. Once every few weeks, he got off one stop early on purpose. The longer route reminded him that convenience can sometimes hide nearby places from us. Losing a few minutes had helped him discover a shop, a craft, and stories that had always been only one stop away.
translation:
ハルトは毎朝同じバスで学校へ行き、校門に最も近い停留所で降りていました。ところが道路工事でその停留所が一週間使えなくなり、一つ前で降りて約八分余分に歩く必要が生じました。朝の習慣をいつも同じにしたいハルトは不満でした。

初日は急いで歩き、周囲をほとんど見ませんでした。二日目は雨で歩みが遅くなり、時計を修理する小さな店に気づきました。窓には背の高い時計、丸い時計、毎時木の鳥が出る時計など、たくさんの古い時計が並んでいました。学校から遠くないのに、店の存在を知りませんでした。

翌朝、五分早く家を出て店の前で立ち止まると、年配の店主が扉を開けながら、学校へ行く前に少し見ていってよいと声をかけてくれました。店は四十年続いており、安いデジタル機器は買い替えやすいため時計を修理する人は減ったものの、家族が何十年も大切にしてきた時計を持ってくる客は今もいるそうです。

一週間の間にハルトはさらに二度立ち寄り、機械式時計が小さな歯車で針を動かす仕組みや、贈り物、結婚祝い、祖父母の思い出として残された時計の話を聞きました。工事が終わるとバスは元の経路へ戻りました。

短い通学路に戻れたことはうれしかったのですが、ハルトは完全には以前の習慣へ戻りませんでした。数週間に一度、わざと一つ前の停留所で降りるようになったのです。便利さは、ときに近くにあるものを見えなくすることがあります。数分を失ったことで、ずっと一停留所先にあった店、技術、そして物語を発見できたのでした。

title: The Lost Photograph
passage:
While helping clean his aunt's house, Koji found a small black-and-white photograph under a drawer. It showed six people standing in front of a wooden building. Nobody in the picture looked familiar to him, and there was no name on the front. Koji almost placed it in a box of old paper, but his aunt asked him to keep it until they knew what it was.

They looked at the back and found a date written in pencil: 1968. There was also one word, ‘Hoshikawa,’ which was the name of a nearby district. Koji's aunt called his grandmother. She could not identify everyone, but she recognized the wooden building as an old community hall that had been pulled down before Koji was born. She suggested asking Mr. Abe, a neighbor who had lived in the area since childhood.

Mr. Abe studied the photograph carefully. After a minute, he smiled. Two of the people were his older brothers. The group had been volunteers who organized a summer festival. The wooden hall was where they stored drums and lanterns. Mr. Abe explained that the festival stopped for several years after the hall closed, but younger residents later started it again in a different park. He had not seen a picture of the old hall for a long time.

Koji scanned the photograph and made a digital copy. His aunt gave the original to Mr. Abe because his family appeared in it. With permission, Koji also sent the scan to the local community center. A staff member added it to a small online collection of neighborhood history, along with the date and information Mr. Abe had provided.

Koji was surprised by how much information had come from one photograph with almost no writing on it. The image itself had not explained the story. The story appeared only when several people shared what they knew. He realized that old objects can be like unfinished questions. A date, a place name, a memory, and a conversation can connect them to a larger history.
translation:
叔母の家の片付けを手伝っていたコウジは、引き出しの下から小さな白黒写真を見つけました。木造の建物の前に六人が立っていますが、知っている顔はなく、表に名前もありません。古紙の箱へ入れようとすると、叔母は正体が分かるまで取っておこうと言いました。

裏を見ると、鉛筆で『1968』と書かれ、『星川』という近くの地区名もありました。叔母が祖母へ電話すると、全員の顔は分からないものの、建物はコウジが生まれる前に取り壊された昔の公民館だと分かりました。さらに、子どもの頃から地域に住む阿部さんへ聞いてみることになりました。

阿部さんは写真をじっと見てから笑顔になりました。写っている二人は彼の兄たちで、夏祭りを運営していたボランティアの仲間でした。木造の会館には太鼓や提灯を保管していたそうです。会館が閉じた後、祭りは数年間中止されましたが、若い住民が別の公園で再開したことも教えてくれました。

コウジは写真をスキャンしてデジタル化しました。叔母は原本を阿部さんへ渡し、許可を得てスキャン画像を地域センターにも送りました。職員は、阿部さんから聞いた日付や情報とともに、地域史の小さなオンライン資料へ加えました。

ほとんど文字のない一枚の写真から、これほど多くの情報が出てきたことにコウジは驚きました。写真そのものが物語を語ったわけではありません。複数の人が知っていることを持ち寄った時に物語が現れたのです。古い物は未完成の問いのようなものかもしれません。日付、地名、記憶、会話が結びつくことで、より大きな歴史へつながるのです。

title: A Lunch Without Plastic
passage:
Mao's class decided to study how much single-use plastic they used during lunch. For five school days, they placed clean plastic wrappers, small sauce containers, and disposable spoons in a separate box. They did not include dirty food waste. At the end of the week, the box was much fuller than most students had expected.

The class wanted to reduce the amount, but their teacher asked them not to make rules immediately. First, they needed to understand why the plastic was being used. They made a list. Some students bought yogurt that came with a plastic spoon. Others used individually wrapped snacks. Several students brought small sauce packets because they were easy to carry and did not leak. The plastic had not appeared for one single reason.

Instead of trying to remove everything at once, the class chose three small changes. Students who often ate yogurt could keep a washable spoon in their lunch bag. Families could use small reusable containers for sauce when it was convenient. The school shop also agreed to sell one type of snack in a larger package so friends could share it rather than buying several small packages. Nobody was required to follow every suggestion.

After two weeks, the class collected plastic again. The amount was about one third lower. The students were pleased, but they also noticed that some kinds of packaging could not easily be changed. One student needed food in a sealed package because of an allergy, and another bought lunch at school on days when his family was busy. The class decided that reducing waste should not make lunch difficult or unsafe for anyone.

Mao said the project changed the way she thought about environmental action. Before, she imagined a perfect solution that everyone should follow. Now she understood that real change often comes from many small choices, and those choices must fit different people's needs. The goal was not to prove that the class could use no plastic at all. The goal was to use less where it made sense and keep learning from the results.
translation:
マオのクラスは、昼食でどれくらい使い捨てプラスチックを使っているか調べることにしました。五日間、きれいな包装、ソース容器、使い捨てスプーンなどを別の箱に集めました。食べ物のごみは含めませんでしたが、週末には予想以上に箱がいっぱいになりました。

減らしたいと考えた生徒たちに、先生はすぐ規則を作るのではなく、まず『なぜ使われているのか』を調べようと言いました。ヨーグルトに付くスプーン、個包装のお菓子、持ち運びやすく漏れにくい小さなソース袋など、理由は一つではありませんでした。

そこで一度に全部をなくそうとせず、三つの小さな変更を試しました。ヨーグルトをよく食べる生徒は洗えるスプーンを弁当袋に入れる。可能な家庭はソースを小さな再利用容器に入れる。売店では、友達同士で分けられる大きめの包装のお菓子を一種類販売する。すべてを強制することはしませんでした。

二週間後にもう一度集めると、プラスチックは約三分の一減っていました。一方で、変えにくい包装もあると分かりました。アレルギーのため密封食品が必要な生徒や、家族が忙しい日に学校で昼食を買う生徒もいます。ごみ削減のために誰かの昼食を不便・危険にしてはいけないとクラスは考えました。

マオは、環境への取り組みに対する考え方が変わったと言いました。以前は、全員が守る完璧な方法を想像していましたが、実際の変化は多くの小さな選択から生まれ、それぞれの事情に合う必要があります。目標はプラスチックを完全にゼロにすることではなく、無理のない部分から減らし、結果を見ながら学び続けることでした。

title: The Small Light in the Hallway
passage:
The second floor of Aya's apartment building had a long hallway with three ceiling lights. All three stayed on from evening until morning. One of Aya's neighbors wondered whether so much light was necessary late at night, when very few people used the hallway. He suggested turning off two lights after midnight to save electricity.

The idea sounded reasonable, but another neighbor was worried about safety. She often returned from work after midnight and did not want the hallway to become dark. The building manager did not want to choose between saving energy and making people feel unsafe. Instead, he asked residents to test different lighting arrangements for one month.

During the first week, they turned off two lights after midnight. The hallway was still visible, but the ends were quite dark. Several residents said they did not like it. In the second week, they kept two lights on and turned off only the middle one. This was better, but the light was uneven. In the third week, the manager installed a small motion sensor near one of the lights. Two lights stayed on at a lower brightness, and the third became bright only when someone entered the hallway.

The residents preferred the third plan. People arriving late could see clearly, while the hallway used less electricity during quiet hours. The sensor was not expensive, but the manager still checked the electricity bill to make sure the change was useful. After two months, the building had used slightly less power than during the same period the previous year. The difference was small, yet the system was kept because residents also liked the softer light.

Aya found the process interesting. At first, the question had seemed simple: should the lights be on or off? The experiment showed that there were more choices between those two extremes. By testing several options, the residents found a solution that considered both energy use and safety. Aya learned that practical problems are often easier to solve when people stop arguing about only two choices and begin looking for a third one.
translation:
アヤの住む集合住宅の二階には長い廊下があり、天井灯が三つありました。三つとも夕方から朝まで点灯していました。ある住民が、深夜は通る人が少ないのだから二つ消して節電してはどうかと提案しました。

もっともらしい案でしたが、別の住民は安全を心配しました。仕事で真夜中を過ぎて帰ることがあり、暗い廊下は困るというのです。管理人は節電と安心のどちらか一方を選ぶのではなく、一か月間いくつかの照明方法を試すことにしました。

一週目は深夜に二灯を消しました。歩ける明るさは残りましたが、廊下の端がかなり暗くなり不評でした。二週目は中央だけ消す方法を試しましたが、明るさにむらが出ました。三週目、管理人は一つの照明に小さな人感センサーを付けました。二灯は低い明るさで点灯し、誰かが入ると三灯目が明るくなる仕組みです。

住民は三つ目の方法を最も気に入りました。遅く帰ってもよく見え、静かな時間帯の電力も減らせます。管理人は実際に効果があるか請求額も確認し、二か月後、前年同時期よりわずかに使用量が減っていました。差は大きくありませんでしたが、柔らかな明るさも好評だったため続けることになりました。

アヤにとって面白かったのは、最初は『つけるか消すか』だけに見えた問題に、その中間の選択肢があったことでした。いくつか試すことで、省エネと安全の両方を考えた方法を見つけられました。実際の問題では二つの案だけで争うより、第三の方法を探すことで解決しやすくなることがあると学んだのです。
